Fields, Capacitors & Particle Physics — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

mcqs.q: A proton consists of which quarks?
options: udd
uud
uds
uuu

mcqs.q: In β⁻ decay, the exchange particle is:
options: Photon
W⁻ boson
Gluon
Z boson

mcqs.q: When does an electron behave as a wave?
options: Electrons are always waves and only look like particles at low energy.
Electrons are sometimes waves and sometimes particles depending on the temperature of the apparatus.
Gravitational potential energy is negative because gravity does negative work.
In experiments that probe wave properties (e.g. diffraction through a crystal); in particle-like experiments it behaves as a particle.

mcqs.q: If the distance between two masses doubles, what happens to the gravitational force between them?
options: It quarters — gravitational force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
It halves — gravitational force is inversely proportional to distance.
It doubles — more distance means more space for gravity to act through.
Electrons are sometimes waves and sometimes particles depending on the temperature of the apparatus.

mcqs.q: Why is gravitational potential energy near a planet treated as negative?
options: Gravitational potential energy is negative because gravity always points downwards.
Electrons are sometimes waves and sometimes particles depending on the temperature of the apparatus.
Because the zero is defined at infinity; objects bound to the planet have lower (negative) potential energy than at infinity.
Gravitational potential energy is negative because gravity does negative work.
